tips.title: Metals give, non-metals take
tips.body: A metal **loses** electrons to form a **positive** ion; a non-metal **gains** them to form a **negative** one. The group number tells you how many: group 1 loses one, group 7 gains one, group 2 loses two, group 6 gains two.

tips.title: Say electrostatic, and say between
tips.body: An ionic bond is the **strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions**. Writing "strong bonds" without naming the force, or without saying between what, loses the mark every time.

tips.title: Conducting means ions moving, not electrons
tips.body: Ionic compounds conduct when **molten or dissolved**, because the **ions** are then free to move. They do not conduct as solids because the ions are locked in the lattice. Electrons are not the carriers here.

tips.title: Read the charge off the group
tips.body: Group 1 forms **1+**, Group 2 **2+**, Group 6 **2−** and Group 7 **1−**. The group number gives the charge without counting electrons each time, and the charges then give the formula: magnesium chloride must be $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ because 2+ needs two 1− ions to balance it.

why.matters:
An atom with an incomplete outer shell is unstable, and bonding is what atoms do about it. But the electron bookkeeping is not the useful part. The useful part is that **which kind of bond forms decides every property you can measure** — melting point, whether it conducts, whether it dissolves, whether it shatters.

Ionic bonding is the first of the three, and its answer is a **giant lattice**: not pairs of ions but millions, each one pulled at from every direction by its opposite.

examples.title: Salt and sugar
examples.body:
Two white crystals on the same shelf, and you can tell them apart with a frying pan. Sugar begins to **caramelise at about 160 °C**. Salt sits there: it does not melt until **801 °C**, which no kitchen can reach.

Sugar is **molecules**, with only weak forces between them, and those forces are all that has to be overcome. Salt is a **giant ionic lattice** held by strong electrostatic attraction in every direction, and melting it means overcoming millions of them at once. The difference you can see is the difference in the bonding.

props.caption: Two white crystals, five times apart in temperature

visual.alt: Two bars in proportion: salt melting at eight hundred and one degrees Celsius against sugar beginning to caramelise at about one hundred and sixty, the difference between a giant ionic lattice and separate molecules

examples.title: Why the salt crystal does not conduct and the brine does
examples.body:
Charge only flows if something charged can **move**. In a salt crystal the ions are locked in the lattice: they are charged, and they are going nowhere, so a dry crystal is an insulator.

Melt it or dissolve it and the lattice comes apart. The same ions are now free to move, and the salt conducts. That is why a meter dipped in water measures conductivity to judge how pure it is — what it is really counting is dissolved ions — and why the carriers here are **ions** rather than the electrons in a wire.

visual.alt: A table of salt in three states: as a solid crystal the ions are fixed in the lattice and it does not conduct, while molten or dissolved the ions are free to move and it does

examples.title: Why a furnace is lined with magnesium oxide
examples.body:
Salt melts at 801 °C. Magnesium oxide, which is built the same way, does not melt until **2852 °C** — hot enough to line the inside of a furnace and still be there in the morning.

Both are giant ionic lattices, so the difference is in the **ions**. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry twice the charge of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and are smaller, so every attraction in the lattice is far stronger. Double the charges and the same structure becomes a refractory brick.

visual.alt: A giant ionic lattice of alternating positive and negative ions, each one attracted to its neighbours in every direction, which is why melting one means overcoming millions of attractions at once

steps.title: Why atoms bond
steps.body:
Atoms react to get a **full outer shell**, like the noble gases. Metals in Groups 1 and 2 have one or two outer electrons and **lose** them. Non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 are one or two short and **gain** them. Losing or gaining electrons turns an atom into an **ion**, a charged particle.

There are three types of strong chemical bond: **ionic** between a metal and a non-metal, **covalent** between non-metals, and **metallic** between metal atoms. This topic is ionic.

steps.text: Loses its one outer electron
Left with 2,8, a full outer shell
It is now Na⁺: 11 protons, 10 electrons, charge 1+

check.prompt: Which atom will lose electrons when it forms an ion?
check.solution: Magnesium has two outer electrons to lose. Oxygen and fluorine gain; neon already has a full shell.

steps.title: Forming ions: sodium chloride
steps.body: Sodium gives its outer electron to chlorine. Sodium becomes **Na⁺** (2,8) and chlorine becomes **Cl⁻** (2,8,8). The dot-and-cross diagram shows the outer shells only, with the transferred electron drawn as a cross among the dots.

visuals.alt: Dot-and-cross diagram for sodium chloride: sodium loses one electron to chlorine, giving Na+ and Cl-

visuals.problem: Describe the dot-and-cross diagram for sodium chloride, NaCl

steps.text: Na is 2,8,1 and Cl is 2,8,7: draw the outer shell only, one cross on the sodium and seven dots on the chlorine
Move the sodium's cross into the chlorine's outer shell, which then holds eight electrons: seven dots and one cross
steps.note: the cross shows where the electron came from

steps.text: The sodium has no outer electrons left, so its full 2,8 shell underneath becomes the outer shell
Draw square brackets round each ion with the charge outside: [Na]⁺ and [Cl]⁻
steps.note: no brackets or no charge, no mark

check.prompt: What is the charge on a magnesium ion?
check.solution: Magnesium, 2,8,2, loses two electrons: 12 protons, 10 electrons, charge 2+.

steps.title: Magnesium oxide: two electrons move
steps.body: Group 2 metals lose two electrons and Group 6 non-metals gain two, so the ions are Mg²⁺ and O²⁻: charges of 2+ and 2−. Because the charges are equal and opposite, one of each makes a neutral compound, MgO. Work it the same way every time: electrons in the outer shell, how many move, what charge that leaves.

visuals.alt: Dot-and-cross diagram for magnesium oxide: magnesium loses two electrons to oxygen, giving Mg 2+ and O 2-

steps.text: Mg is in Group 2: two electrons in its outer shell. O is in Group 6: six, and room for two more
Both electrons move from Mg to O. Mg is left with a full shell underneath and a charge of 2+
O now has eight in its outer shell and a charge of 2−
2+ and 2− cancel, so the formula is MgO, one of each
steps.note: Compare NaCl, where one electron moves and the charges are 1+ and 1−

check.prompt: Which compound has ions with charges 2+ and 1−?
check.solution: Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻. Two chloride ions are needed per magnesium ion: MgCl₂.

steps.title: The ionic bond and the lattice
steps.body: An **ionic bond** is the strong **electrostatic attraction** between oppositely charged ions. The ions do not pair up: every positive ion is surrounded by negative ions and every negative by positives, in a regular repeating pattern called a **giant ionic lattice**. The forces act in **all directions**.

visuals.alt: A giant ionic lattice: alternating positive and negative ions in a regular grid

check.prompt: What holds the ions together in sodium chloride?
check.solution: Electrostatic attraction between the opposite charges. Shared electrons are covalent; the sea of electrons is metallic.

markScheme.description: Electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions

options: Shared pairs of electrons between the sodium and chlorine atoms
Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions
A sea of delocalised electrons surrounding the sodium ions
Weak intermolecular forces between sodium chloride molecules

steps.title: Formulae from charges
steps.body:
The charges in a compound must **cancel**. Magnesium chloride: Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻, so **MgCl₂**. Aluminium oxide: Al³⁺ and O²⁻; the lowest common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6, so two Al³⁺ and three O²⁻: **Al₂O₃**. A quick method: swap the charge numbers over, drop the signs, **then simplify to the lowest ratio**. Mg²⁺ with O²⁻ gives Mg₂O₂ by swapping, which simplifies to MgO.

Exams also give you a picture of part of a lattice and ask for the formula. Count each kind of ion in the picture, then simplify the ratio. A diagram with 4 calcium ions and 8 chloride ions is 4:8, which simplifies to 1:2, so the formula is CaCl₂. The formula is always the simplest whole-number ratio, never the number you counted.

Some ions are groups of atoms with a single overall charge: sulfate SO₄²⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻, hydroxide OH⁻, ammonium NH₄⁺. They behave like one ion. When you need more than one of them, put it in brackets: Mg²⁺ with two NO₃⁻ is Mg(NO₃)₂.

steps.text: Ca²⁺ and Br⁻
One 2+ needs two 1−
CaBr₂
The diagram shows 6 magnesium ions and 12 chloride ions
Ratio 6:12 simplifies to 1:2
Formula MgCl₂, which also matches the charges: one 2+ against two 1−

visuals.problem: Dot-and-cross diagram for calcium chloride, CaCl₂

steps.text: Calcium in the middle with 2 outer electrons drawn as crosses
One chlorine either side, each with 7 outer electrons drawn as dots
One cross moves to each chlorine, so each gains one electron
Three brackets: [Ca]²⁺ in the middle and [Cl]⁻ on each side, each chlorine showing 8 electrons

check.prompt: Write the formula of the compound formed from Al³⁺ and O²⁻.
check.solution: Two Al³⁺ (6+) balance three O²⁻ (6−): Al₂O₃.

steps.title: The three states, and where the particle model stops
steps.body:
Solid, liquid and gas differ in how the particles are arranged and how much energy they have. Melting and boiling happen when the particles gain enough energy to overcome the forces holding them together, so the **stronger those forces, the higher the melting and boiling points**. That is why a giant ionic lattice melts at hundreds or even thousands of degrees and a simple molecular solid such as ice melts at 0 °C.

State symbols record which state a substance is in: **(s)** solid, **(l)** liquid, **(g)** gas, **(aq)** dissolved in water.

The simple particle model has limits you can be asked for: it draws particles as **solid, inelastic spheres**, it shows **no forces between them**, and it treats every particle as the same size, when real particles are atoms, ions or molecules of different sizes with real forces between them.

visuals.problem: Sodium chloride melts at 801 °C and boils at 1413 °C. Write it with state symbols at 20 °C, 1000 °C and 1500 °C.

steps.text: 20 °C: below the melting point, so NaCl(s)
1000 °C: between melting and boiling, so NaCl(l)
1500 °C: above the boiling point, so NaCl(g)

check.prompt: Which is a limitation of the simple particle model?
check.solution: The model shows particles as identical solid spheres with no forces between them. Real particles differ in size and do attract each other.

markScheme.description: No forces between the particles are shown

options: It shows the particles as different colours
It cannot show a solid, only liquids and gases
It shows no forces between the particles
It shows too many particles to count

steps.title: Properties of ionic compounds
steps.body:
- **High melting and boiling points**: many strong electrostatic forces to overcome in all directions, so a lot of energy is needed.
- **Do not conduct when solid**: the ions are fixed in the lattice.
- **Conduct when molten or dissolved in water**: the lattice breaks down and the ions are free to move and carry charge.
- Many dissolve in water, and the solution conducts because the ions separate and are free to move.

steps.text: Solid NaCl: ions locked in place, no
Molten NaCl: ions free to move, yes
NaCl solution: ions free to move, yes

check.prompt: Why does molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?
check.solution: In an ionic compound the charge carriers are the ions, and they can only move once the lattice has melted.
options: The electrons are free to move
The ions are free to move
The atoms are free to move

steps.title: Your turn: explain in mark-scheme language
steps.body: Exam explanations follow a shape: **structure, forces, energy**. Name the structure (giant ionic lattice), name the forces (strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, in all directions), then say what that means for energy (a lot needed to overcome them). Practise saying it out loud.

visuals.problem: Why does magnesium oxide have a high melting point?

steps.text: Giant ionic lattice
Strong electrostatic forces between Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, in all directions
Lots of energy needed to overcome them
So the melting point is high

check.prompt: Which phrase would an examiner reject in an explanation of melting point?
check.solution: "The bonds are strong" does not say what kind of bonds or between what. The other three are mark-scheme phrases.
options: The forces act in all directions
A lot of energy is needed to overcome the forces
Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions

steps.title: Going deeper: comparing compounds, and the limits of the model
steps.body:
Magnesium oxide melts at 2852 °C, sodium chloride at 801 °C. Both are ionic, so the difference is in the **ions**: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry twice the charge of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and are smaller, so the electrostatic attraction is stronger and more energy is needed.

Top questions also ask about **models**. A dot-and-cross diagram shows electron transfer but not the lattice. A ball-and-stick model shows the arrangement but exaggerates the gaps between the ions, and the sticks make the bonds look like rigid rods rather than electrostatic attraction acting in all directions. A space-filling model shows the packing but hides the ions inside. A two-dimensional drawing of the lattice shows one flat layer; the real lattice is three-dimensional, with each ion surrounded by ions above and below as well.

visuals.alt: A giant ionic lattice with alternating charges, the arrangement no dot-and-cross diagram can show

check.prompt: Which factor makes the attraction between ions in magnesium oxide stronger than in sodium chloride?
check.solution: 2+ and 2− against 1+ and 1−: double the charge, and the ions are smaller too.
options: The ions carry a greater charge

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Metals lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metals gain to form negative ions. Group number tells you the charge.
- Ionic bond: strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, in a giant lattice.
- Formulae: charges must cancel. MgCl₂, Al₂O₃.
- High melting points; conduct only when molten or dissolved, because ions must be free to move.
- Bigger charges and smaller ions mean stronger attraction.

questions.prompt: Ionic bonding happens between
questions.solution: Metals lose electrons to become positive ions; non-metals gain them to become negative ions. The opposite charges attract.
options: a metal and a noble gas

questions.prompt: What is the charge on a sodium ion?
questions.solution: Sodium is in Group 1, so it loses one electron and becomes Na⁺, with a charge of 1+.

questions.prompt: A chlorine atom has the electronic structure 2,8,7. What is the electronic structure of a chloride ion, Cl⁻?
questions.solution: A chloride ion has gained one electron, filling the outer shell: 2,8,8, the same as argon.

questions.prompt: Write the formula of calcium chloride. Calcium forms Ca²⁺ ions and chlorine forms Cl⁻ ions.
questions.solution: The charges must cancel: one 2+ needs two 1−. CaCl₂.

questions.prompt: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity?
questions.solution: The ions are there, but locked in the lattice. Conduction needs charged particles that can move, which happens when the compound is molten or dissolved.

markScheme.description: Ions cannot move in the solid

options: It has no ions until it is dissolved
The ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move

questions.prompt: Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point.
questions.solution: Three marking points: giant ionic lattice; strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions, acting in all directions; a large amount of energy needed to overcome them. "Bonds" alone is not enough; say what kind.

markScheme.description: Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions

criteria.text: Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice
Strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions, acting in all directions
A large amount of energy is needed to overcome them

questions.modelAnswer: Sodium chloride has a giant ionic lattice structure. The oppositely charged sodium and chloride ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction, which act in all directions throughout the lattice. A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these many strong forces, so the melting point is high.

questions.prompt: Write the formula of aluminium oxide. Aluminium forms Al³⁺ ions and oxygen forms O²⁻ ions.
questions.solution: Two Al³⁺ give 6+, three O²⁻ give 6−. Al₂O₃.

questions.prompt: In the dot-and-cross diagram for magnesium oxide, how many electrons move from the magnesium atom to the oxygen atom?
questions.solution: Magnesium is 2,8,2 and loses both outer electrons; oxygen is 2,6 and gains two.

questions.prompt: Magnesium oxide melts at 2852 °C and sodium chloride melts at 801 °C. Both are ionic compounds. Explain the difference in melting points.
questions.solution: Level-marked. Level 3 compares both compounds, names the ions with charges, links charge and size to the strength of attraction, and ends with the energy conclusion.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points about the two lattices, ion charges, attraction strength, and energy, not linked
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct account of the two lattices, ion charges, attraction strength, and energy with some links
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, complete comparison of the two lattices, ion charges, attraction strength, and energy using the correct terms

criteria.text: Both are giant ionic lattices with electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions
Magnesium oxide contains Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions; sodium chloride contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻
The 2+ and 2− ions have a greater charge, so the electrostatic attraction between them is stronger
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are also smaller than Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so the ions are closer together, which strengthens the attraction further
More energy is needed to overcome the stronger forces in magnesium oxide
Therefore magnesium oxide has the higher melting point

questions.modelAnswer: Both compounds are giant ionic lattices in which oppositely charged ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction. Magnesium oxide is made of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, whereas sodium chloride is made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. The ions in magnesium oxide carry twice the charge, so the electrostatic attraction between them is much stronger. They are also smaller, so the charges are closer together, which strengthens the attraction further. More energy is needed to overcome the forces in magnesium oxide, so its melting point is higher.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a limitation of a dot-and-cross diagram of sodium chloride?
questions.solution: A dot-and-cross diagram shows one pair of ions and the electron transfer. It says nothing about the lattice, the relative sizes of ions, or the fact that each ion is surrounded by several others.
options: It does not show the charges on the ions
It does not show that the ions form a giant three-dimensional lattice
It does not show which electrons are transferred

questions.prompt: Element X forms a compound with the formula X₂SO₄. The sulfate ion is SO₄²⁻. What is the charge on an X ion?
questions.solution: One sulfate ion carries 2−, so two X ions must carry 2+ between them: each X ion is 1+.

questions.prompt: A metal M forms M³⁺ ions. In its oxide, how many oxide ions, O²⁻, are there for every two M³⁺ ions? Give your answer as a number.
questions.solution: Two M³⁺ carry 6+. Each O²⁻ carries 2−, so **3** are needed to give 6−: M₂O₃.

questions.prompt: Explain why potassium bromide conducts electricity when it is molten but not when it is solid.
questions.solution: Say ions, not electrons: ionic compounds never conduct by electrons moving.

criteria.text: Potassium bromide contains K⁺ and Br⁻ ions
In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice by strong electrostatic forces and cannot move
When molten the lattice has broken down and the ions are free to move
Conduction needs charged particles that can move and carry the charge, so only the molten compound conducts

questions.modelAnswer: Potassium bromide is made of K⁺ and Br⁻ ions. In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in a giant lattice by strong electrostatic forces, so they cannot move. When the compound is molten, the lattice has broken down and the ions are free to move. Electrical conduction needs charged particles that are free to move and carry the charge through the substance, so only the molten compound conducts.

questions.prompt: Which pair of ions both have the same electronic structure as neon, 2,8?
questions.solution: Na (2,8,1) loses one electron: 2,8. F (2,7) gains one: 2,8. Cl⁻, K⁺ and S²⁻ are all 2,8,8, like argon.

questions.prompt: Which state symbol shows sodium chloride dissolved in water?
questions.solution: (aq) means aqueous: dissolved in water. (l) is the molten liquid, (s) the solid, (g) a gas.

questions.prompt: An element is in Group 6 of the periodic table. What charge does its ion have?
questions.solution: Group 6 atoms have six outer electrons and gain two to fill the shell, giving a charge of 2−.

questions.prompt: Write the half equation for a sodium atom forming a sodium ion.
questions.solution: Sodium loses one electron: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻. The electron is written on the right because it is given away.

markScheme.description: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻, with the electron on the right

questions.prompt: Calcium chloride is made from Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. In its dot-and-cross diagram, how many chlorine atoms are drawn, and how many electrons does each receive?
questions.solution: Calcium loses two electrons, and each chlorine atom can only take one, so two chlorine atoms are needed: CaCl₂.

markScheme.description: Two chlorine atoms, one electron each

options: Two chlorine atoms, one electron each
Two chlorine atoms, two electrons each

questions.prompt:
A student tests four unknown solids and records their melting points and whether they conduct electricity.

| Solid | Melting point in °C | Conducts when solid | Conducts when molten |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 801 | No | Yes |
| B | 114 | No | No |
| C | 1085 | Yes | Yes |
| D | 1610 | No | No |

Identify the solid that is an ionic compound. Explain your choice, and say what type of structure each of the other three solids has.
questions.solution: Use the table: quote the melting point and both conduction results, and say what each rules out. Graphite is the one giant covalent structure that does conduct, but it has a very high melting point and conducts as a solid, which D does not.

markScheme.description: Its high melting point shows strong forces between particles in a giant structure
It does not conduct when solid because the ions are fixed in the lattice, but conducts when molten because the ions are then free to move
B is simple molecular: low melting point and never conducts
C is a metal: it conducts as a solid
D is giant covalent: very high melting point and does not conduct in either state

criteria.text: Its high melting point shows strong forces between particles in a giant structure
It does not conduct when solid because the ions are fixed in the lattice, but conducts when molten because the ions are then free to move
B is simple molecular: low melting point and never conducts
C is a metal: it conducts as a solid
D is giant covalent: very high melting point and does not conduct in either state

questions.modelAnswer: Solid A is the ionic compound. Its high melting point shows a giant structure with strong forces between the particles. It does not conduct as a solid because its ions are held in fixed positions, but it conducts when molten because the ions are then free to move. B has a low melting point, so it is made of simple molecules. C conducts as a solid, so it is a metal. D has a very high melting point and does not conduct in either state, so it is a giant covalent structure such as silicon dioxide.

questions.prompt: A diagram of part of an ionic lattice shows 9 calcium ions and 18 fluoride ions. Write the formula of the compound.
questions.solution: 9:18 simplifies to 1:2, so CaF₂. The formula is the simplest ratio, not the count in the picture.

questions.prompt: Calcium forms Ca²⁺ ions and the nitrate ion is NO₃⁻. Write the formula of calcium nitrate.
questions.solution: One 2+ needs two 1−. The nitrate ion is a group of atoms, so it goes in brackets: Ca(NO₃)₂.

examTechnique.body: Ionic bonding questions range from one-mark formulae to six-mark explanations. The explanation marks are for specific phrases: giant ionic lattice, strong electrostatic forces of attraction, oppositely charged ions, in all directions, lots of energy to overcome. Dot-and-cross diagrams need the outer shell only, a bracket or box round each ion, and the charge written outside it.
examinerErrors: Saying ionic compounds conduct because electrons move. It is the ions.
Writing "strong bonds" without saying electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions.
Leaving off the square brackets round each ion or the charge outside the bracket, or drawing the transferred electron with the same symbol as the atom that received it.
Getting a formula wrong by matching one ion to one ion regardless of charge, such as MgCl.
Saying molecules of sodium chloride. Ionic compounds have no molecules.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names the structure, the particles, and the forces in the right words every time, compares compounds by ion charge and size, writes formulae from charges without hesitation, and can say what each model of a lattice leaves out.
